title: Rommel retreats from Alamein

facts.text: Early on 2 November 1942 the Eighth Army opened Operation Supercharge, a fresh push aimed at Tel el Aqqaqir, the Axis defensive base on the Rahman track. The 9th Armoured Brigade attacked at 06:15 and lost most of its tanks, but the line held open.

Rommel saw that his army was bleeding to death and began to pull back. At 13:30 on 3 November he received a message from Hitler ordering him to stand fast, to yield not a yard of ground, and to show his troops no other road than that to victory or death.

Rommel wrote that the order demanded the impossible. 'We were completely stunned,' he wrote, and for the first time in the African campaign he did not know what to do. He obeyed and ordered his men to hold their positions.
On the morning of 4 November the British broke through. Rommel wrote that by early afternoon enemy armour had burst a 19 kilometre hole in his front, and he had no reserves left.
The Afrika Korps was down to a few dozen working tanks against hundreds of British tanks. Rommel's own figures put the Germans at 36 tanks on 4 November, from 249 at the start of the battle.

That same day General Wilhelm Ritter von Thoma, commander of the Afrika Korps, was captured west of El Alamein after surrendering to men of the 10th Hussars. He was taken to Montgomery's headquarters, where Montgomery met him and later invited him to dinner.

At 17:30 on 4 November Rommel ordered a general retreat without waiting for Hitler's reply, writing that superior orders could no longer count and he had to save what could be saved. Hitler's approval did come, but Rommel wrote that it arrived much too late in the day.

With little transport, much of the Italian infantry was left behind, and the Italian Ariete, Trento and Bologna divisions were destroyed. Thousands of Axis soldiers were taken prisoner, and the total for the battle came to about 30,000.

Alamein was the first great British land victory over the German army. On Sunday 15 November 1942 church bells rang across Britain to mark it, the first time most people had heard them in over two years; they had been kept silent as an invasion alarm.
At the Mansion House in London on 10 November 1942, Churchill said: 'Now this is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning.'

On 8 November 1942 American and British troops landed in French North Africa in Operation Torch. Rommel's army was now caught between two Allied forces and began a long retreat of more than a thousand miles west toward Tunisia.

declassified.fact: Rommel's escape got help from the weather. Around midday on 6 November rain began to fall on the desert, and by the next day waterlogged ground and empty fuel tanks had stranded the British 1st and 7th Armoured Divisions. The British attempt to trap his army near Mersa Matruh came up short.

body:
Hitler's order was victory or death. Rommel chose neither.

4 November 1942. The morning after Hitler ordered him to yield not a yard of ground, the British broke through at El Alamein. By early afternoon, Rommel wrote, enemy armour had burst a 19 kilometre hole in his front, and he had no reserves left.

By his own figures the Germans were down to 36 tanks, from 249 at the start of the battle. That same day the commander of the Afrika Korps, General Wilhelm Ritter von Thoma, surrendered to men of the 10th Hussars. Montgomery met him and later invited him to dinner.

At 5:30 p.m., Rommel ordered a general retreat without waiting for Hitler's reply. With little transport, much of the Italian infantry was left behind. About 30,000 Axis soldiers were taken prisoner in the battle.

It was the first great British land victory over the German army. On 15 November church bells rang across Britain, the first time most people had heard them in over two years.
addons: If you had been in Rommel's place, would you have obeyed the order?

video.note: Desert Victory (1943), British Ministry of Information documentary with film shot by the Army Film and Photographic Unit; Crown copyright expired, public domain (PD-UKGov on Wikimedia Commons; 480p copy from Brian's Source Film folder). From the film's breakthrough section, which its narrator introduces at 44:37 to 44:53 ('the entire weight of their armour was in readiness... it sailed through the gap. Its purpose was simple, to destroy Rommel's armour'); the narrator is silent from 44:53 to 48:12, apart from a shouted 'Fire!' in the scene at 47:24, which is left out. Clip uses 45:49.65 to 45:53.25 (Grant tanks charging through smoke as a shell bursts), 47:18.80 to 47:21.35 (a tank racing forward in its own dust), 45:44.45 to 45:45.55 (two Shermans crossing the desert), 45:20.60 to 45:26.00 (a line of tanks rolling forward) and 45:40.20 to 45:41.90 (a tank passing toward the horizon). The film does not date each shot, so the caption says it shows the end of the battle. Left out: the shots of German officers with binoculars at 45:28 to 45:33 (captured enemy newsreel) and any shot under the narration. Sound: the film's own soundtrack under these shots (engines, shell bursts and gunfire; no narration by speech recognition, no music by spectrogram), cut with the picture and normalized to -16 LUFS.
video.hook: Rommel retreated without waiting for Hitler.
